item.title: Resonance-induced quantum non-Gaussian states below criticality
item.description:
Worth a look theory — Weak periodic qubit modulation below criticality ( extλ=1/√2<λ_c=1) prepares Floquet states with Wigner negativity volume up to ∼0.96 and negative Wigner complexity ∼0.12, far more resilient to loss than superradiant ground states.

Grade 0.440 · 1.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum information with Rydberg atoms” · Daniel J. Nader, Pavel Stránský, Jorge Chávez-Carlos, Pavel Cejnar, Radim Filip

Figure

Evolution of quantum non-Gaussian indicators during and after an adiabatic modulation ramp for parity-conserving (η→=z→) and parity-breaking (η→=x→) qubit modulation, showing growth and persistence of target Floquet fidelity and Wigner negativity.

Asks

Can weak spin-frequency modulation generate complex, robust quantum non-Gaussian states in the Quantum Rabi Model at coupling strengths below the critical point?

Before

Reaching quantum non-Gaussian states required ramping coupling across critical point λ_c=1, yielding superradiant ground states highly fragile against bosonic loss.

But

Numerical simulation with bosonic Fock space truncated at N=50; valid in the adiabatic limit where state populations approximately follow instantaneous Floquet states.

Tools

Quantum Rabi Model (QRM) · adiabatic Floquet ramp protocol · Poincaré–Birkhoff resonance conditions · Lindblad master equation · Wigner negativity volume analysis

Code. https://github.com/djuliannader/RabiModel

Abstract

The Quantum Rabi Model (QRM), consisting of a single qubit coupled to a harmonic oscillator, provides a paradigmatic platform for exploring critical phenomena investigated for their applications in quantum technologies. In the superradiant phase of the QRM with coupling strength above the critical point, the bosonic ground state exhibits temporally stable quantum non-Gaussian features. However, the quantum non-Gaussian features of such superradiant ground states can be fragile against loss during preparation. Here, we show that persistent quantum non-Gaussian features can instead be realized below the critical point through weak periodic qubit modulation. We analyze an adiabatic ramp protocol in which the modulation amplitude is gradually increased, allowing the system to approximately follow the instantaneous Floquet state. When the modulation period is tuned close to Poincaré-Birkhoff resonances, the resulting state exhibits pronounced quantum non-Gaussian features in the directly measurable Wigner function with a complex phase-space structure that is considerably more robust against loss than that of the superradiant ground state. The protocol of adiabatic ramps provides an attractive route for generating long-lived quantum non-Gaussian effects below the critical point.

item.title: Performance of Fusion-Based Quantum Computing with Imperfect Photon Indistinguishability
item.description:
Long shot new result — Photon distinguishability threshold decreases from 0.136% to 0.080% under Shor(2,2) encoding for all-photonic resource state preparation, but remains comparable for repeat-until-success (RUS) generation at 0.256% unencoded and 0.271% encoded.

Grade 0.434 · 1.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “photonic qubits, linear-optical computing and boson sampling” · Katia Hakem, Grégoire de Gliniasty, Nathan Shettell, Paul Hilaire, Stephen C. Wein

Figure

Six-ring resource state graph. Vertices represent qubits in |+⟩ and edges represent CZ gates; highlighted vertices show the stabilizer generator K1=Z6X1Z2.

Asks

How does partial photon distinguishability during resource state generation and linear-optical fusion measurements affect the fault tolerance and logical encoding benefits of fusion-based quantum computing architectures?

But

First-order distinguishability expansion in D, dual-rail encoding with ideal photon-number-resolving detectors, specific to 6-ring fusion networks.

Tools

Orthogonal bad-bit distinguishability noise model · 6-ring fusion network · Shor(2,2) code encoding · Monte Carlo fault-tolerance simulations · Repeat-until-success emitter entangling gates

Abstract

Fusion-based quantum computation (FBQC) is a promising route to fault-tolerant photonic quantum computing, connecting small entangled resource states through linear-optical fusion measurements. While logical encoding can substantially improve resilience to photon loss, whether these benefits extend to other noise remain an open question. In this work, we show that this is not generally the case when accounting for partial photon distinguishability during resource state generation and fusion measurement. We develop hardware-motivated noise models to capture these effects and investigate their impact on fault tolerance in the 6-ring fusion network. We compare unencoded and Shor(2,2)-encoded resource states prepared using all-photonic and emitter-assisted repeat-until-success (RUS) schemes. For the all-photonic construction, encoding reduces the distinguishability threshold from 0.136% to 0.08%. In contrast, the RUS construction tolerates more distinguishability, with comparable unencoded and encoded thresholds (0.256% and 0.271%, respectively). These results expose a fundamental limitation of evaluating logical encodings under idealized resource-state assumptions and demonstrate that resource-state generation can critically determine the fault tolerance of photonic architectures.

item.title: Frequency Multiplexing of Purcell-Enhanced Optically Coherent NV Centers
item.description:
Long shot new result — Multiple NV centers embedded in a monolithic diamond Sawfish nanocavity show inhomogeneous optical linewidths down to 19 MHz sustained over minutes, approaching the 13 MHz lifetime limit. Gas-tuning the cavity into resonance with the zero-phonon line enhances emission by 16.8(1.4)%.

Grade 0.432 · 1.4σ above the day's baseline · matched “cavity QED, atom-photon interfaces and quantum networks” · Alok Gokhale, Marco E. Stucki, Malo Bezard, Maarten H. van der Hoeven, Kilian Unterguggenberger, Gregor Pieplow, Tommaso Pregnolato, Julian M. Bopp, Laura Orphal-Kobin, Tim Schröder

Figure

PLE spectra and linewidth scaling of cavity-embedded NV centers. (c) Integrated PLE counts versus laser detuning showing individual NV resonances with a 19 MHz minimum linewidth (inset). (d) Measured inhomogeneous linewidths (blue diamonds) and extracted homogeneous linewidths (red circles) versus excitation power, approaching the 13 MHz lifetime limit (grey dashed line).

Asks

Can multiple spectrally distinct NV centers be integrated into a single nanophotonic cavity while preserving lifetime-limited optical coherence and stable charge states?

Before

Cavity Purcell factors up to 70 were achieved previously (Smith 2024), but nanophotonic integration routinely degraded optical coherence, preventing coherent frequency multiplexing.

But

Measured at approximately 5 K. Purcell enhancement inferred cumulatively over an estimated 15(4) randomly positioned and oriented NV centers rather than deterministically positioned single emitters.

Tools

monolithic diamond Sawfish photonic crystal nanocavity · cryogenic gas tuning (nitrogen condensation and laser desorption) · photoluminescence excitation (PLE) spectroscopy · finite-element method (FEM) simulations in JCMsuite

Abstract

Integrating optically coherent quantum emitters into nanophotonic structures is key to scalable quantum networks. Realizing them with nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond is hindered by the degradation of optical coherence accompanying nanofabrication. Here, we overcome this challenge by integrating multiple NV centers into a monolithic diamond photonic crystal nanocavity while preserving near-lifetime-limited optical coherence. We observe linewidths as narrow as 19 MHz, enabling the frequency multiplexing of spectrally distinct NV centers within a common cavity mode, while maintaining charge-state stability over several minutes under resonant excitation. Tuning the cavity into resonance with the NV zero-phonon line enhances the optical emission, consistent with Purcell enhancement predicted by finite-element simulations. Additionally, individual cavities can be independently brought into resonance with NV zero-phonon lines on the same chip. These results combine bulk-like optical coherence with frequency multiplexing and cavity-enhanced emission, establishing a scalable nanophotonic platform for NV-based quantum network nodes.
